draft.title: Peace in Buddhism and Hinduism
card: Buddhism
Suffering comes from craving, the constant wanting that is never satisfied. Peace grows as a person lets go of craving through practices such as meditation and following the Eightfold Path.
Buddhists also practise compassion (karuna), a wish to relieve the suffering of others. This turns inner calm into peaceful action towards other beings.
Hinduism: ahimsa
Ahimsa means non-harm, in thought, word and deed. It asks Hindus to avoid violence towards all living things.
Hinduism: union
Hindus also seek the deep peace of moksha, release from the cycle of rebirth. It comes through union with Brahman, the ultimate reality.
draft.remember: Buddhism: peace through letting go of craving and acting with compassion. Hinduism: peace through ahimsa and union with Brahman.

a.q: Which teaching best shows how Buddhism links peace to the ending of suffering?
opts: Peace grows as craving is overcome
Peace comes from union with Brahman
Peace comes from practising ahimsa towards all
Peace comes from release into moksha alone
a.why: In Buddhism, craving is the source of suffering, so letting it go brings peace. Union with Brahman is a Hindu idea, so it is the tempting wrong answer here, since it is also about peace.
a.clue: Which option names the cause of suffering in Buddhism?

b.q: Priya, a Hindu, refuses to harm insects in her garden and speaks gently even when angry. Which teaching is she following?
opts: Ahimsa, non-harm in thought, word and deed
Karuna, compassion to relieve others' suffering
Overcoming craving by following the Eightfold Path
Moksha, release from the cycle of rebirth
b.why: Priya avoids harm in action and in speech towards living things, which is ahimsa. Compassion (karuna) is tempting because it also cares for others, but it is a Buddhist teaching about relieving suffering, and Priya is a Hindu avoiding harm.
b.clue: Think of the Hindu teaching about not causing harm.

a.best: Peace grows as craving is overcome

b.best: Ahimsa, non-harm in thought, word and deed

problems.detail: The why calls karuna a Buddhist teaching and rules it out because Priya is Hindu. Karuna (compassion) is also valued in Hinduism, so that reasoning is misleading. It is wrong because it is about relieving suffering, not avoiding harm.
The clue 'Think of the Hindu teaching about not causing harm' repeats the question's 'harm' and points straight to the only option saying 'non-harm', so it gives the answer away.
